scenes.tts: Take an invented population of one hundred individuals, with a per capita growth rate of point two per day. After ten days, you might expect three hundred. If nothing stops it, there are about seven hundred thirty nine. Growth compounds. Each new individual starts adding individuals of its own.
scenes.caption: Take an invented population of 100 individuals, with a per capita growth rate of 0.2 per day. After ten days, you might expect 300. If nothing stops it, there are about 739. Growth compounds. Each new individual starts adding individuals of its own.
scenes.visual: bars: 100 at day 0; a guessed 300 bar crossed out; the real bar grows to 739 at day 10
scenes.narration: Take an invented population of 100 individuals, with a per capita growth rate of 0.2 per day. After ten days, you might expect 300. If nothing stops it, there are about 739. Growth compounds. Each new individual starts adding individuals of its own.

scenes.tts: Call the number of individuals big N. Call the per capita rate little r. Growth each day is little r times big N, so more individuals add more. A constant little r gives a constant doubling time. Here it is about three point four seven days, whether the population holds one hundred or one hundred thousand.
scenes.caption: Call the number of individuals N. Call the per capita rate r. Growth each day is r times N, so more individuals add more. A constant r gives a constant doubling time. Here it is about 3.47 days, whether the population holds 100 or 100,000.
scenes.visual: exponential curve in this sketch; equal doubling intervals of 3.47 days marked along the time axis
scenes.narration: Call the number of individuals N. Call the per capita rate r. Growth each day is r times N, so more individuals add more. A constant r gives a constant doubling time. Here it is about 3.47 days, whether the population holds 100 or 100,000.

scenes.tts: Real populations meet a brake. Each individual typically gets less food, space or shelter, so births fall or deaths rise. The logistic model puts the brake on the per capita rate. That rate falls in a straight line, from little r when big N is near zero, to zero at big K. Big K is the carrying capacity.

scenes.tts: Total growth is that per capita rate times big N. At low big N, there are few individuals to multiply. Near big K, each one adds almost nothing. So the product is greatest in the middle, at big K over two. There it is fifty individuals per day.

scenes.tts: Now run both models from a hundred individuals. At day ten, the exponential model gives seven hundred thirty nine. The logistic model gives about four hundred fifty one. They agree at first, then part. By day twenty, the exponential model predicts five thousand four hundred sixty, and the logistic about eight hundred fifty eight. These numbers are illustrative, not measured for any species.
scenes.caption: Now run both models from 100 individuals. At day ten, the exponential model gives 739. The logistic model gives about 451. They agree at first, then part. By day twenty, the exponential model predicts 5,460, and the logistic about 858. These numbers are illustrative, not measured for any species.
scenes.visual: both curves from 100: exponential leaves the top of the frame, logistic bends toward K; day 10 and day 20 values marked

By day twenty, the exponential model predicts 5,460, and the logistic about 858. These numbers are illustrative, not measured for any species.

scenes.tts: Big K is an equilibrium, not a ceiling. If big N starts above big K, the model predicts decline back toward it. If big N starts below, the continuous model rises smoothly and never overshoots. Real populations have age structure, time lags and a big K that changes. Any of these can produce overshoot. Keep the rule: the per capita rate falls as big N rises.
